title: Chemical signalling
summary: How cells communicate using signalling chemicals and receptors, from quorum sensing in bacteria to hormone receptors that trigger signal transduction pathways or change gene expression.

keyterms.definition: A signalling chemical that binds specifically to a receptor's binding site.
A protein with a binding site for a specific signalling chemical; binding changes the receptor's shape and triggers a response in the cell.
Cell signalling in bacteria where an autoinducer accumulates with population density, triggering coordinated gene expression, e.g. bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.
A signalling chemical secreted into the blood by an endocrine gland, with distant effects on target cells; may be an amine, protein or steroid.
A signalling chemical released from a neuron that diffuses across a synaptic gap, with localized effects on the adjacent cell.
A small protein secreted by cells for local signalling, especially to coordinate the immune response.
A receptor spanning the plasma membrane, with hydrophobic amino acids in the membrane, that binds hydrophilic ligands which cannot enter the cell.
A receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus that binds hydrophobic ligands such as steroid hormones; the complex can alter gene expression.
The sequence of events inside a cell, triggered by a ligand binding to its receptor, that results in a cellular response.
A transmembrane receptor that, when a ligand binds, activates a G protein inside the cell to relay the signal, e.g. the epinephrine receptor.
A molecule inside the cell, such as cyclic AMP (cAMP), that relays and amplifies the signal from a receptor to the cell's response.
A transmembrane receptor that phosphorylates tyrosine residues when its ligand binds, starting a signalling cascade, e.g. the insulin receptor.
Regulation in which a response reduces the original signal or stimulus, stabilizing the system.
Regulation in which a response amplifies the original signal, causing a rapid, escalating change.

questions.prompt: In cell signalling, what is a ligand?
options: A protein that spans the membrane
A signalling chemical that binds to a specific receptor
An enzyme that produces cAMP
A channel that opens in response to voltage
questions.explanation: The ligand is the signalling chemical; the receptor is the protein with a binding site specific to that ligand.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of quorum sensing in Vibrio fischeri in order.
items: Each bacterium releases an autoinducer signalling molecule
Autoinducer concentration rises as population density increases
Above a threshold, autoinducer binds to receptors in the bacteria
The bacterial population emits light together
questions.explanation: Autoinducer only reaches a high concentration when many bacteria are present, so light is produced only when there are enough bacteria to make it worthwhile.

questions.statement: Quorum sensing allows bacteria to change their behaviour only when their population density is high.
questions.explanation: Because each cell releases the signal, its concentration indicates population density; gene expression changes only when a threshold concentration is reached.

questions.prompt: Match each category of signalling chemical to its description.

pairs.right: Transported in blood to distant target cells
Crosses a synaptic gap to an adjacent cell
Small protein for local signalling, e.g. in immunity
Trigger neurotransmitter release and muscle contraction

questions.explanation: These are functional categories in animals. Hormones act at a distance, while neurotransmitters and cytokines act locally; Ca2+ acts as a signal inside cells.

options: Insulin
Epinephrine (adrenaline)
Oestradiol
Glucagon
questions.explanation: Oestradiol is a steroid made from cholesterol. Insulin and glucagon are proteins (polypeptides); epinephrine is an amine.

questions.text: Steroid hormones are hydrophobic, so they cross the plasma membrane and bind to ___ receptors.
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic ligands diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus. Hydrophilic ligands need transmembrane receptors.

questions.statement: Hormones have localized effects, whereas neurotransmitters have effects throughout the body.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: hormones travel in the blood and can act on distant targets; neurotransmitters cross a tiny synaptic gap, so their effects are localized.

questions.prompt: Why do hydrophilic signalling molecules such as insulin bind to transmembrane receptors?
options: They cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the plasma membrane
They are too small to bind intracellular receptors
Transmembrane receptors are found only in the nucleus
They are broken down in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic ligands cannot cross the bilayer, so they bind to the extracellular part of a transmembrane receptor; the receptor's hydrophobic amino acids anchor it in the membrane.

questions.text: Small proteins secreted for local signalling, especially in the immune system, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Cytokines are protein signals between nearby cells, for example between cells of the immune system during an infection.

questions.prompt: What makes a receptor specific to one signalling chemical?
options: It is made of lipid
It is found in every cell of the body
It is always located in the nucleus
Its binding site is complementary in shape and chemical properties to the ligand
questions.explanation: Like an enzyme's active site, the receptor's binding site fits only ligands of a particular shape and charge distribution, so only target cells with the receptor respond.

questions.prompt: What is a signal transduction pathway?
options: The movement of a hormone through the blood
The sequence of events inside a cell triggered by a ligand binding to a receptor
The diffusion of a neurotransmitter across a synapse
The synthesis of a hormone in an endocrine gland
questions.explanation: Binding changes the receptor's shape, which triggers a chain of reactions inside the cell that leads to a response.

questions.prompt: How does acetylcholine change the membrane potential of a postsynaptic cell?
options: It enters the cell and binds to DNA
It activates a G protein, producing cAMP
It is pumped into the cell by active transport
It binds to a receptor that is an ion channel, opening it so Na+ ions enter
questions.explanation: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Binding opens the channel, positive ions (mainly Na+) flow in and the membrane depolarizes.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of epinephrine signalling in a liver cell in order.
items: Epinephrine binds to a receptor on the plasma membrane
The receptor changes shape and activates a G protein
The G protein activates an enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP
Glycogen is broken down to glucose
questions.explanation: Epinephrine never enters the cell; its signal is relayed by a G protein and amplified by the second messenger cAMP, giving a rapid response such as releasing glucose.

questions.statement: Epinephrine enters liver cells and binds to receptors in the nucleus.
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is hydrophilic, so it binds to a G protein-coupled transmembrane receptor on the cell surface; cAMP carries the signal inside.

questions.text: In epinephrine signalling, cyclic AMP acts as a ___ messenger.
questions.explanation: The hormone is the first messenger outside the cell; cAMP is the second messenger inside the cell that relays and amplifies the signal.

questions.prompt: What is the outcome when insulin binds to its receptor?
options: The receptor opens as a Na+ channel
Tyrosine kinase activity starts a cascade that moves vesicles with glucose transporters to the membrane
Insulin enters the nucleus and alters transcription
cAMP is released from the receptor
questions.explanation: The insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase: binding causes phosphorylation of tyrosines, triggering a cascade that inserts glucose transporters into the plasma membrane, increasing glucose uptake.

questions.prompt: Match each signalling chemical to its type of receptor.

pairs.right: Intracellular receptor that alters gene expression

questions.explanation: Hydrophilic ligands (acetylcholine, epinephrine, insulin) use different transmembrane receptors; the hydrophobic steroid oestradiol uses an intracellular receptor.

questions.prompt: What effect does oestradiol have on cells in the hypothalamus?
options: It inhibits all hormone secretion
It activates a G protein on the cell surface
It binds intracellular receptors and increases GnRH secretion
It thickens the endometrium
questions.explanation: Oestradiol binds to receptors inside hypothalamus cells and changes gene expression, increasing GnRH secretion. Progesterone acts on endometrium cells to maintain the uterus lining.

questions.statement: When a steroid hormone binds to its intracellular receptor, the complex can bind to DNA and change gene expression.
questions.explanation: The hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, promoting or inhibiting transcription of specific genes, e.g. progesterone in endometrium cells.

questions.prompt: Distinguish negative from positive feedback in a signalling pathway.
options: Negative feedback reduces the original signal and stabilizes; positive feedback amplifies it
Negative feedback amplifies the signal; positive feedback reduces it
Both always return the system to a set point
Positive feedback only occurs in bacteria
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response reduces the signal, keeping conditions stable; in positive feedback the response increases the signal, causing rapid change until an end point.
